name: The Köppen Climate Classification
statement: The Köppen system sorts the world's climates into five main letter-coded groups based on annual and seasonal patterns of temperature and precipitation.
statementAccent: sorts the world's climates into five main letter-coded groups
meaning: Wladimir Köppen, trained in both climatology and botany, designed the system so climate boundaries would roughly track natural vegetation zones. Each location gets a short code (Af, Cfb, Dfb) built from a main group letter plus subtype letters describing precipitation seasonality and temperature severity.
mechanism: A location’s type is derived from monthly temperature and precipitation normals: the first letter (A tropical, B arid, C temperate, D continental, E polar) is set by temperature and aridity thresholds, and subsequent letters (f for no dry season, s for dry summer, w for dry winter; a/b/c/d for temperature) refine it using further threshold rules.

examples.text: Singapore is a classic Af example, with at least 60 mm of rain in every month and consistently high temperatures.
Moscow is classified Dfb, with warm-to-hot summers and long, cold winters.
Köppen first published the system in 1884 and revised it substantially in 1918 and 1936; Rudolf Geiger later modified it, giving the commonly used "Köppen–Geiger" designation.

whyItMatters: It remains the most widely used climate classification globally, underpinning textbooks, agricultural planning, biogeography, and climate-change tracking by letting researchers compare climates across regions with a compact, standardised code.
limits: Because it relies solely on monthly temperature and precipitation averages, it can miss microclimates, extreme events, and finer vegetation distinctions; the boundary thresholds are somewhat arbitrary, and different revisions can place borderline locations in different categories.
misreadings: The codes are sometimes read as directly describing biomes, when they are strictly climate categories derived from statistical thresholds — correlated with vegetation but not identical to ecological classification.
origin: Devised by German-Russian climatologist Wladimir Köppen, first published in 1884 (with a fuller version around 1900) and revised through 1936; later updated by Rudolf Geiger.
